title: A one-sided spiral, NGC 4654
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 4654, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 4654 · Virgo Cluster · constellation Virgo · about 72 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, D. Thilker, J. Lee and the PHANGS-HST Team

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Month, July 2026 (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: One side of this spiral galaxy has a crisp, rounded edge, while its other side trails off. NGC 4654, about 72 million light-years away in Virgo, is being pushed and pulled by forces acting across whole galaxies.

It lies in the Virgo Cluster, a crowded, massive cluster of galaxies filled with thin, hot gas. As NGC 4654 races through that gas, the pressure squeezes its leading edge and drags a long tail of its own gas out behind it, beyond the edge of this picture. Its stars are unevenly spread too: the leading arm is rich in stars and gas, while the opposite arm has noticeably few.

That pressure alone probably isn’t enough to explain the lopsidedness. A fly-by of the neighboring galaxy NGC 4639 about 500 million years ago is thought to have stripped gas from one side too. Even so, NGC 4654 still forms nearly two Suns’ worth of stars each year, seen as bright pink bubbles.
scale: Using the source’s listed field of view (2.63 × 2.53 arcminutes) and its distance of about 72 million light-years, the frame spans roughly 55083 × 52988 light-years. Its light set out about 72 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble’s cameras through six filters, from ultraviolet to near-infrared, including one for glowing hydrogen. The color assigned to each filter isn’t published.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and the colors are assigned, so the eye would not see this palette.
filters: 657 nm · Optical H-alpha + N II (Hubble WFC3)

explore: NGC 4654 is an intermediate spiral, between barred and unbarred spirals, with a weak bar at its core. The data come from programs connecting galaxies’ gas with their star formation.
alt: A spiral galaxy with one sharp, rounded edge and a frayed opposite side, dotted with pink star-forming bubbles.
